cards.prompt: Why is CA practically never on the table when designing a distributed system?
cards.answer: Because a network partition is a fault, not something you design away. Since you can't assume the network stays intact 100% of the time, partition tolerance is non-negotiable — leaving only CP or AP.

cards.prompt: Under CAP, partition tolerance is not a design decision but a ____ that will eventually occur in any real network.
cards.explanation: Reframing partitions as faults is what collapses the 'three choose two' story into a simple CP-versus-AP decision.

cards.prompt: Nodes A and B both store x = 1. User A writes x = 2 on node A. User B then reads x from node B and receives 1. What did the system just demonstrate?
options: It chose availability over consistency by serving a stale value
It chose consistency over availability by returning the latest value
It achieved CA by avoiding the partition entirely
It lost the write, since node B never received x = 2
cards.answer: Availability won: node B answered immediately with the old value instead of coordinating to return the fresh one.
cards.explanation: Any answer is a trade-off — stale-and-fast means AP, fresh-but-maybe-blocking means CP.

cards.prompt: Your teammate suggests answering reads with the newly written value even if node B must wait for cross-node coordination before replying. Which side of the CAP trade-off is the system taking, and what does it risk?
cards.answer: That's the CP path: consistency is preserved by coordinating, but if a node can't reach its peer the read may stall or fail, so availability takes the hit.
cards.explanation: The same read returning 1 instead of 2 would be the AP answer — fast, but possibly stale.

cards.prompt: Explain like I'm 10: why is 'pick two out of three' a misleading way to describe CAP?
cards.answer: One of the three — partition tolerance — isn't something you get to pick, because networks break on their own, like a phone line going dead mid-call. You can't promise the line will never fail, so you must design as if it will. That leaves only the real choice: when the line does break, do you keep answering (AP) or keep everyone seeing the same data (CP)?

cards.prompt: In the two-node example where x is updated to 2 on node A: what does it mean if node B answers a read with 2, and what does it mean if it answers with 1?
cards.answer: Returning 2 means the system stayed consistent; returning 1 means it stayed available. Either way the design has picked its side of the CP/AP trade-off.
cards.explanation: The post's point is that 'which is right?' has no universal answer — it depends on what the application needs.
